newsitem.title: USA: US, EU meat talks continue down to wire.
newsitem.headline: US, EU meat talks continue down to wire.

text.p: Talks between the United States and the European Union to settle a trans-Altantic dispute over meat and poultry inspection methods appeared on Thursday to be spilling over into the Easter holiday weekend.

But U.S. meat and poultry industry officials said it would take another miracle for negotiators to reach an agreement in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks by a rapidly approaching April 1 deadline.
"It's looking like it's going to take something pretty extraordinary to get any agreement by April 1," said Joel Brandenberger of the National Turkey Federation.

"The consensus of the meat people is that we're far apart on most of the issues, and that it is unlikely that there will be an agreement reached by April 1," said Len Condon of the American Meat Institute.

Negotiators have been meeting in Washington all week to resolve the years-old dispute which could threaten several hundreds of millions of dollars worth of trade in meat, poultry, dairy, eggs and pet food.

At the core of the issue is how Washington and Brussels deal with the different U.S. and EU meat and poultry safety inspection methods, and the impact on trade. An agreement would allow each side to accept products from the other even if their inspection methods differ.

Agriculture Department officials held separate briefings with the meat, poultry and dairy sectors throughout the day Thursday to put together a package of counter proposals to send back to EU negotiators.
An EU official said negotiators were expecting to receive the U.S. proposal Thursday evening and that another meeting was scheduled for Friday.
What will happen on April 1 if an agreement has not been reached is still unclear.
The EU has said it would implement new veterinary and sanitary controls for imports on April 1, and the United States has said it would retaliate for any loss of access to EU markets.

Some $50 million worth of U.S. poultry shipments to the EU could be curtailed if the EU adopts new standards, and Washington could potentially halt the imports of over $200 million worth of European pork.
Some $350 million worth of U.S. pet food exports to Europe could also be affected, but industry officials said most of the issues pertaining to pet food appear to have been resolved.
Industry officials said the administration is still debating what its move should be if no agreement is reached, and that immediate action is not likely on April 1.
"There's a wide range of options ... It's all up in the air now ... It's way too soon to say what's going to happen as of April 1," said an industry source.
